intro.say: Your dog tilts its head when you talk. Squirrels pretend to bury nuts. And the cobra in the snake charmer's basket can't even hear the music.
Animals do strange things every single day, and most of us never find out why.
So here are ten weird animal behaviors, finally explained by science.

scenes.say: Say a word your dog knows, and there's a good chance its head tips to one side. For years, nobody had actually studied why.
Then, in 2021, researchers in Budapest watched forty dogs as their owners asked them to fetch toys by name.
Seven of them were gifted word learners, all border collies, that could remember the names of many toys.
Those gifted dogs tilted their heads forty three percent of the time when they heard a toy's name. The typical dogs did it just two percent of the time.
And each dog kept tilting to the same side, like being left or right handed. The researchers think the tilt is a sign of processing: the dog is matching the word to a picture of the toy in its head.
It may also have to do with how the brain handles sound on one side, a bit like people tilting their heads when they try to picture something they remember.
A single squirrel can bury up to three thousand nuts in one season. But some of those holes are empty on purpose.
Biologist Michael Steele noticed that gray squirrels sometimes dig a hole, pretend to drop a nut in, cover it up, and walk away with the nut still in their mouth.
In his 2008 study, these fake burials made up around thirteen percent of caching, and they happened more often when other squirrels were watching.
It's a decoy. Any thief who saw the show digs up nothing, while the real nut ends up somewhere else.

Squirrels also dig up nuts and bury them again somewhere new, sometimes several times. And when people played thief in experiments, the squirrels quickly switched to harder hiding spots and more fake holes.

chapters.title: Why birds can eat chili peppers

scenes.say: The burn of a chili comes from capsaicin, which triggers a pain receptor in mammals called T R P V one.
Birds have a version of that receptor that barely reacts to capsaicin. To them, the hottest pepper doesn't burn at all.
That's no accident. Mammals chew seeds and destroy them, but birds swallow peppers whole and pass the seeds intact.
Field studies in Arizona found curve-billed thrashers dropping chili seeds right under shrubs, exactly where new plants grow best. The spice keeps the wrong animals away and lets the right ones in.
It's also why some people mix chili powder into birdseed. The birds eat as usual, while squirrels and other mammals get a mouthful of fire.
It looks like the cobra is swaying to the music. But snakes have no external ears and no ear drums.
They do sense sound, mostly low vibrations that travel through the ground and into their jaw bones. The high notes of a flute barely register.
What the cobra really sees is a large object moving in front of it, and to a snake, that looks like a threat.
So it rises, spreads its hood, and follows every move of the swaying pipe. The music isn't for the snake. It's for the crowd.
A good charmer stays just out of striking range and keeps the pipe moving, so the snake keeps tracking it instead of striking.

chapters.title: How owls turn their heads 270 degrees

scenes.say: An owl can turn its head up to two hundred seventy degrees in either direction. It has to, because its tube-shaped eyes can't move in their sockets.
Humans have seven neck vertebrae. Owls have fourteen.
When a Johns Hopkins team scanned owl necks in 2013, they found the holes that carry a key artery are about ten times wider than the artery itself, giving it room to move.
They also found blood reservoirs under the jaw that fill up while the head is turned, so the brain and eyes keep getting blood. Twist your own neck that far and you could tear an artery.
On top of that, owls have small connections between the main arteries in the neck, so if one route gets pinched, blood can take another.

chapters.title: Why flamingos stand on one leg

scenes.say: Flamingos can rest, and even sleep, standing on one thin leg for long periods.
In 2017, researchers in Atlanta found the pose holds itself up passively, with almost no muscle effort.
In one test, a dead flamingo placed on one leg stayed upright on its own. On two legs, it didn't.
And the joint that looks like a backward knee is actually the ankle. The real knee is hidden up under the feathers. Folding one leg may also save body heat in cold water.
That idea is now interesting to engineers, because a leg that balances without effort could help build better robots and prosthetic limbs.

chapters.title: Why crows never forget a face

scenes.say: At the University of Washington, researchers wore a caveman mask while they trapped and tagged a few wild crows.
Later, anyone walking around campus in that mask got scolded and mobbed, even though they did nothing to the birds.
On one walk, forty seven of fifty three crows scolded the mask, far more than the birds that were ever caught.
The grudge spread to other crows and lasted for years. A neutral mask got almost no reaction at all.
Later, brain scans of crows looking at a threatening face lit up areas linked to fear, much like in our own brains.
Scientists argued about zebra stripes for well over a century. The strongest answer today is surprisingly small: flies.
In a 2019 study, horse flies approached zebras just as often as plain colored horses.
But near the zebras they failed to slow down, flew past, or bumped right into them instead of landing.
When the researchers put striped coats on horses, far fewer flies landed on the stripes. Fewer landings means fewer bites and fewer diseases.
And when a fly did land, it stayed on a horse for about ten seconds, but on a zebra for only about one.
Many cats press their paws into blankets, pillows, or your lap. People call it making biscuits.
It starts on day one. Nursing kittens knead their mother's belly to get the milk flowing.
Many cats keep the habit as adults, often when they feel safe and relaxed.
There's a second reason too. Cats have scent glands in their paw pads, so kneading leaves their smell behind. When your cat kneads you, it may be quietly marking you as its own.
Holding on to baby behaviors into adulthood even has a name: neoteny. Kneading is one of the cutest examples.
Deer are most active at dawn and dusk, and their eyes are built for dim light.
Compared to us, they have far more rods, the cells that work in low light, and at night their pupils open extremely wide.
When headlights suddenly hit those wide open eyes, the deer is effectively blinded. It can't see the car, the road, or a way out.
So it stands still until its eyes adjust. It's not bravery or stupidity. It's anatomy.
Deer eyes also have a mirror-like layer behind the retina. It boosts night vision, and it's the reason their eyes glow back at you in the dark.

outro.say: So which one surprised you most? The squirrel's fake burial, the crows with a grudge, or the dog that tilts its head to think?
